2.1.1 Definition of continuity at a point
A function is called continuous if its graph can be drawn with a pencil without lifting
it from the paper. Formally: a function f is continuous at the point x = a, if
lim x →af(x) = f(a)
This condition contains three requirements: (1)f(a) is defined; (2) lim x →af(x) exists;
(3) the limit equals the function value. The function is discontinuous at aifitis not
continuous at a.
lim x →a −f(x) = lim x →a + f(x) = f(a)

Equivalent form: the left-hand and right-hand limits are equal to each other and
equal to the function value at the point.
• Strategy for checking continuity at a point (Problem-Solving Strategy

defined — the function is discontinuous at a, the check is complete.
• Step 2: compute lim x →af(x)(if necessary, first compute lim x →a −f(x)and lim
x →a + f(x)). If the limit does not exist (is not a real number) — the function is
discontinuous at a.
• Step 3: compare f(a)and lim x →af(x). If lim x →af(x) ̸= f(a) — the function is
discontinuous at a; if equal — continuous at a.
• Continuity on an interval: f is continuous on the open interval (a, b)ifit is
continuous at each of its points; on the closed interval [a, b] — if additionally continu-
ous from the right at point a: lim x →a + f(x) = f(a), and continuous from the left at
point b: lim x →b −f(x) = f(b).
2.1.2 Types of Discontinuities
Iff is discontinuous at point a, the discontinuity is classified as follows (Definition,
§2.4):
• Removable discontinuity: lim x →af(x) exists and equals a real number L, but
f(a)is not defined or f(a) ̸= L — a ”hole” in the graph.
• Jump discontinuity: lim x →a −f(x)and lim x →a + f(x) both exist and are finite,
but lim x →a −f(x) ̸= lim x →a + f(x) — the parts of the graph do not connect.
• Infinite discontinuity: lim x →a −f(x) = ±∞and/or lim x →a + f(x) = ±∞— a
discontinuity at a vertical asymptote.
• Oscillatory discontinuity: the function oscillates, not approaching any single
value — for example, f(x) = sin(1/x)asx →0; lim x →0f(x) does not exist.
Not all discontinuities neatly fit into these categories — this is a convenient classifi-
cation of three typical cases.
2.1.3 Continuity of Elementary Functions, Polynomials, Rational Functions
Theorem 2.8 (continuity of polynomials and rational functions):
polynomials and rational functions are continuous at each point of their domains.
Theorem 2.10: trigonometric functions are continuous on their entire domains.

Theorem 2.11 (Intermediate Value Theorem, important for engineering):
a function continuous on a closed bounded interval takes every intermediate value.

theorem guarantees existence, but not uniqueness.

x < 2; 5, if x = 2; 3x −1, if x > 2} is continuous at the point x = 2.
Solution. Left-hand limit: lim x →2 −f(x) = 22 + 1 = 5. Right-hand limit: lim x →
2 + f(x) = 3 · 2 −1 = 5. Value at the point: f(2) = 5. Therefore, lim x →2f(x) = f(2) = 5,
so f is continuous at the point x = 2.

Continuity requires k = lim x →3f(x). Therefore, k = 6.

Exercise 5. Finding the inverse. The drive displacement x is related to the
input voltage V byx(V ) = 0.5 · V + 2, 0 ≤V ≤10. (1) Find the range of x. (2) Find
the inverse function V (x). (3) Explain why the inverse is continuous.

V (x) = 2 · (x −2) = 2x −4, 2 ≤x ≤7. The original function is continuous and strictly
increasing on [0, 10], so its inverse is continuous on [2, 7].

Exercise 10.
Why it’s important that the interval is closed.
Consider the
efficiency model η(v) = v, 0 < v < 10. Does the Weierstrass theorem guarantee
a maximum and minimum?
Solution. The function is continuous, but the interval (0, 10) is open, not closed. The
function approaches 0asv →0+, but never reaches 0; it approaches 10asv →10−, but
never reaches 10. Therefore, the function has neither an absolute minimum nor an
absolute maximum on this domain. The Weierstrass theorem does not apply because
the domain is not closed.

The temperature along a

Exercise 12. Connecting all three ideas. A pressure sensor is modeled by the
function V (p) = √p + 1, 0 ≤p ≤8. (1) Show that V is continuous. (2) Explain why
it has a continuous inverse. (3) Find the inverse. (4) Using the Weierstrass
theorem, specify the minimum and maximum voltage of the sensor.
Solution. (1) The function p + 1 is continuous, and the square root is continuous for
non-negative inputs, so V is continuous on [0, 8]. (2)It is also strictly increasing,
hence one-to-one; therefore, a continuous inverse exists. (3) Start with V = √p + 1;
square both sides: V 2 = p + 1, from which p(V ) = V 2 −1. (4) The voltage range is
obtained at the endpoints: V (0) = 1, V (8) = 3. By the Weierstrass theorem, these
extrema are achieved: Vmin = 1atp = 0andVmax = 3atp = 8. The inverse is defined for
1 ≤V ≤3.
Exercise 13. When the theorem cannot be applied. The cost of constructing
a pipe: C(r) = π ·r2 +1/r, 0 < r ≤5. A student claims: ”The cost is continuous, so
the Weierstrass theorem guarantees a maximum.” Evaluate this statement.
Solution. The function is continuous for r > 0, but the domain (0, 5] is not closed, as
it does not contain r = 0. Asr →0+, we have 1/r →+∞, so C(r) →+∞. Therefore, the
function has no absolute maximum on (0, 5] — it becomes arbitrarily large as r ap-
proaches zero. The student’s reasoning is incorrect: continuity alone is insufficient;
the Weierstrass theorem requires a closed and bounded domain.

Assignment 6.
Designing a continuous sensor model.
A sensor uses the
model S(x) = {a · x + b, if x < 1; 3, if x = 1; x2 + 2, if x > 1}.
Find the condi-
tion on aandb for which S is continuous at x = 1. Specify two possible pairs
(a, b).
Solution. At the point x = 1: the left-hand limit equals a·1+b = a+b; the function value
S(1) = 3; the right-hand limit equals 12 + 2 = 3. Continuity requires all three values to
be equal: a + b = 3. This is the condition on the parameters. Two possible options: (a,
b) = (1, 2)and(a, b) = (2, 1) — in both cases a + b = 3, both branches meet at the point
(1, 3). (The method is similar to exercises 145–149 from the EXTRA material.)

The NOTES explain why mathematical models behave predictably: small changes in
input lead to small changes in output, measurements can sometimes be inverted to
recover unknown quantities, and engineering variables attain maximum and mini-
mum values on finite operating ranges. Key points of the NOTES:
• Informal meaning of continuity (1.1): the graph of a function has no
breaks, jumps, holes, or vertical asymptotes in the domain under consideration. In
engineering terms: if y = f(x) is continuous near x = a, then a sufficiently small
change in the input x produces a small change in the output y.
• Continuity at a point (1.2): lim x →af(x) = f(a); three requirements — f(a) is
defined, the limit exists, the limit equals the value. Equivalent to: lim x →a −f(x) =
lim x →a + f(x) = f(a).
• Continuity on an interval (1.3): on (a, b) — continuity at each point; on [a,
b] — additionally continuity from the right at a and from the left at b(one−sided con-
ditions are needed because outside [a, b] the function may not be defined).
• Algebra of continuous functions (2): if fandg are continuous at a, then f+
g, f −g, c · f, f · gandf/g are continuous at g(a) ̸= 0. Polynomials are continuous every-
where; rational functions are continuous where the denominator is non-zero; expo-
nential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions are continuous on their domains.

GUIDANCE for MIDTERM EXAM Preparation 
 
Important points: 
1. The Midterm Exam will take place on MONDAY, November 2, during the regular Lecture 
hours. 
2. Total duration: 2 hours. 
3. It is a pen-paper Exam. No digital/electronic devices are allowed. No books, no notes. 
Mobile phones and all digital/electronic devices and paper notes/books will be secured 
in your bags. 
4. No restroom (toilet) breaks will be allowed during the Midterm Exam duration. 
5. The Midterm Exam will focus primarily on textbook Chapters 2 (sections 2.1-2.4) and 
Chapter 3 (sections 3.1-3.5, and 3.9 [except for subsection 3.9.3] and the Instructor’s 
NOTES. We assume that you know well the material covered before, in weeks 1-3, which 
was tested in Test 1. 
6. The Midterm Exam will start sharply at the start time of the Lecture class and will end 
after exactly 2 hours.  
7. You must return all the handouts given to you for the Exam (problem sheets, solutions 
sheets, crap paper).  
8. If you finish earlier, you may leave the classroom, but you must have already returned 
all the handouts (see previous point). 
9. What to expect from you, regarding your answers to the Exam problems: The problems 
are meant to test your knowledge of concepts and methods. Showing the mathematical 
procedure, giving clear explanations and the reasoning behind your solution are the 
important aspects that we would like to see in your work. No heavy algebra is required 
for solving the problems. If you get stuck with algebra, just explain clearly what you 
want to do. 
 
The best strategy for preparing for the MIDTERM Exam comprises the following steps: 
• Study the required readings (chapters/sections from textbook) and instructor Notes.  
• Study very well the Lecture presentations and the examples and exercises presented in 
them, because they cover the most important concepts and methods. 
• Study very well the exercises covered in the Practical Sessions. Study very well the 
Independent Study Assignments (ISA).
